title: Reinforcement Learning for Agents - Will Brown, ML Researcher at Morgan Stanley
talk_summary: Will Brown explains how RL (GRPO-style: sample N completions, score them, reinforce higher-scoring ones) is what unlocked reasoning models and could unlock more autonomous agents, and argues the practical near-term lever for AI engineers is 'rubric engineering' — designing rich, multi-signal reward/scoring functions rather than binary pass/fail. He demos a single-file GRPO trainer and a multi-step environment framework, but explicitly says none of this is production-ready advice.

takeaways.technique: Rubric engineering: multi-signal scoring instead of binary pass/fail
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of scoring only 'did it get the answer right', they give partial credit for intermediate properties (correct XML tag, integer format, following structure) so the system gets a dense signal about what 'working' means.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if it gets a certain tag right you give it plus one point... if it has an integer answer that's still the wrong answer... Get some points for that

takeaways.what_they_do: Warns that a scoring model can be gamed — the agent finds a way to get high reward without doing the task — so the reward must be audited against the real goal.
takeaways.evidence_quote: reward hacking is an issue to be very cautious of where the idea is you want to ensure that the the reward model you're using is actually capturing the goal

takeaways.technique: Auto-tune prompts/rubrics against a downstream score (DSPy-style)
takeaways.what_they_do: Treats prompt/rubric improvement as an optimization loop: use a measurable downstream score to bootstrap better prompts or scoring rules, optionally with LM judges designing the rubrics.
takeaways.evidence_quote: autotuning these rubrics or autotuning your prompts with frameworks like DSPI... incorporating LM judges as part of the scoring system

takeaways.technique: Environment abstraction for multi-step agent loops
takeaways.what_they_do: Wraps an existing agent framework as an 'environment' with a defined interaction protocol so a trainer can plug in without touching weights/tokens; the same env can be used for eval and for RL.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can just create this environment thing that the model plugs into and you don't have to worry about the weights or the tokens

takeaways.technique: Trial-and-error is a skill, not a prompt
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues knowledge can go in a prompt but skills (getting good at a task) come from repeated trial and error with feedback — so agents that never retry won't improve.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it is really hard to include a skill in a prompt... a model does get better at a thing... by trial and error
